title: History of the Precepts
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart traces the history of the precepts for a Jukai celebration on Samish Island, framing it with Mary Oliver's poem "When Death Comes." Kanho follows the rules from the Buddha's time, when the Sangha could not agree which to drop and kept even the one against slurping soup, through the Vinaya in India, the Chinese Brahma Net Sutra with its 58 precepts, and Saicho's ordination platform in Japan. Dogen's reformulation into the 16 Bodhisattva precepts follows, understood as practice-realization with no gap between them. Kanho ends by reading the ten grave precepts with the commentaries of Bodhidharma and Dogen, then rereads the tenth when a participant asks.
topics: Taking the precepts as a way of life

sentences.text: *And in the past, penetrating in perfect dharma, is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas, having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, how to taste the truth of the Tathagata.*
Have you started the recording?
I'm so happy that you're all here, because without you, this would not be happening.
It's great to see so many old friends and new friends.
November on Samish Island definitely feels different from our June retreat.
On the other hand, the dark and cold almost feel like an invitation: an invitation to wait for the coming light, the grand reveal, the celebration.
This is truly how I feel today.
This afternoon, there will be a Jukai celebration.
More baby bodhisattvas will be taking the precepts.
In one way, nothing much will change.
People will continue to live their lives, continue to bump into furniture, argue over Thanksgiving turkeys and watch football games.
And yet, in our Soto Zen tradition, the precept ceremony shows up over and over, by itself and as the core of other ceremonies.
Over and over, we are asked to take on the precepts as a way of life, as a way to live by vow.
We should deeply investigate for ourselves what taking the precepts means to us personally.
What does it look like in real life?
Superficially, of course, we can say, "Yeah, no problem, all this makes sense.
I don't run around killing, stealing, etc."
Following the precepts makes great sense for living in community.
However, if we stop there, we deprive ourselves of the potential offered by the precepts.
Yes, we can work on improving our conduct.
We can do a little bit better.
Embracing the precepts on that level is great, don't misunderstand.
As an alternative, maybe it would be better to say in addition, we can create enough space for transformation.
The radical dissolution and reformation of our ethical landscape: what would that look like?
What would that feel like?
My teacher, Norman Fischer, said, in Zen precept practice, the fundamental absolute ground of ethics is being itself.
Because we and the world exist, there are precepts.
Things are, life is, and in this, not being is also included.
A moment of time arising is a moment of time passing.
Being born is the beginning of dying.
This is sad, tragic, and probably impossible for us to fully appreciate.
Yet we can and do feel the immensity of being itself, the strangeness of unbeing.
Grounding our lives in this fundamental truth is the fruit of our practice.
This is where the teaching of no difference between good and evil comes from.
It is essential, but it can't be taken out of context.
Mary Oliver wrote a poem, "When Death Comes."

*When death comes like the hungry bear in autumn, when death comes and takes all the bright coins from his purse to buy me, and snaps the purse shut, when death comes like the measle pox, when death comes like an iceberg between the shoulder plates, I want to step through the door, full of curiosity, wondering what is it going to be like, that cottage of darkness?

And therefore, I look upon everything as a brotherhood and a sisterhood, and I look upon time as no more than an idea, and I consider eternity as another possibility, and I think of each life as a flower, as common as a field daisy, and as singular, and each name a comfortable music in the mouth, tending, as all music does, towards silence.
Each body a line of courage, and something precious to the earth.*
*When it's over, I want to say, all my life, I was a bride married to amazement, I was the bridegroom taking the world into my arms.
When it's over, I don't want to wonder if I have made of my life something particular and real.*
But how did we all get here?
During the Buddha's time, many rules, hundreds of them, were created, often as a direct response to some event or some deed.
On his deathbed, the Buddha said that the Sangha should drop the less important rules.
However, they could not agree which rules were less important than the others, so they kept them all.
Some of them are actually pretty funny.
Like, don't say "zuru, zuru" when you slurp your soup.
Don't bump your neighbor with your elbows.
And so they could not agree to eliminate the non-slurping rule.
At the first Buddhist council, Upali, who was the master of the conduct rules, the Vinaya, listed the rules and they were accepted.
Subsequently, the strict Vinaya rule was followed everywhere in the Buddhist world for hundreds of years.
From the point of view of the Vinaya rules, interactions with others are only important insofar as they affect your consciousness and your personal liberation.
When Buddhism came to China, it was mostly Mahayana Buddhism that took hold.
With its foundation of compassion and the emptiness teachings, a different expression of guidelines was needed.
Confucianism had deeply imprinted a sense of social responsibility.
So the Chinese community expanded the understanding of the Vinaya to express and integrate compassion and social virtue.
This became a hallmark of Zen in China and later Japan.
We follow mind and heart rather than the letter of the Vinaya.
This is very clearly stated in our Zen practice.
So it is quite a different attitude.
Oliver again explains it like this, as a doorway into thanks and silence in which another voice may speak.
*It doesn't have to be the blue iris.
It could be weeds in a vacant lot or a few small stones.
Just pay attention.
Then patch a few words together and don't try to make them elaborate.
This isn't a contest but the doorway into thanks, and the silence in which another voice may speak.*
To China, in the 5th century CE, the Brahma Jala Sutra, the Brahma Net Sutra, was written.
Though it is claimed that it is a translation from the Pali or the Sanskrit language, almost all scholars agree that this was basically another fake sutra that was written in China.
That doesn't mean that it is unimportant.
In fact, it was so important that they had to invent the background story.
So we should respect that.
This sutra contains 58 precepts: 10 major precepts, which are similar to but not exactly the same as the grave precepts in Zen, and 48 minor precepts.
It is important to note that these are not monastic precepts meant just for the monks.
They were written to be practical to both monastics and the lay practitioners.
In Japan, one of the early founders of the Tendai school, Saicho, established in the 8th century an independent ordination platform in which only the 58 precepts were used, not all of the Vinaya.

This seems like a very radical step, but maybe not as much as I thought originally, because in Japan they never did establish the Vinaya ordination as strong as they had been in China, India and other Buddhist countries.
So it wasn't that hard for Saicho to change the ordination in this way.
Dogen, the founder of our Zen school, was originally a Tendai monk, and so he was ordained with those 58 precepts.
But now the question is, how did we get from 58 to 16?
We do follow the 16 Bodhisattva precepts, which include the three refuges, the three pure precepts and the ten grave precepts.
This combination of guidelines is unique to Zen, and probably it was created by Dogen himself.
While all of the 16 precepts existed before, Dogen did reformulate them in the specific way that we still use today.
Never before had the three refuges and the three pure precepts been part of precepts or guidelines.
Thus there was a return to an ethical formulation that extended beyond rules into our hearts and into a greater society.
Lifestyle precepts, specific rules matter and they are important.
On the other hand, the 16 Bodhisattva precepts are completely understood as a religious commitment.
We receive the precepts in shukai, in priest ordination and in transmission.
Dogen understood the 16 precepts mainly on the ultimate, the absolute level: the ultimate expression of Dharma as an expression of Buddha's life.
Dogen saw them as an object of contemplation, almost unknowable, as the koan of our life.
One of Dogen's main religious insights and themes is that practice and realization are not two different things.
As we would say, practice-realization.
They cannot be separated.
If you hear "realization," you might think that is the culmination of practice, and practice is the tool that we use to get there.
But that is not so.
We can make the choice to live by vow.
We can choose to live with practice-realization, no gap in between.
The precepts are the ultimate expression of our own practice.
Often I end my talks with a poem.
Today, however, I will end with a reading of the precepts.
And maybe when we listen, we can think practice-realization.
Every moment of practice is a moment of realization.
Sitting down for zazen reenacts the Buddha's enlightenment.
The only realization is through practice, one continuously, eternally unfolding process.
And the precepts are an outward manifestation of this process.
There must be love, otherwise it's a rule book.
So please listen to the precepts and the commentary that Bodhidharma, the first Zen ancestor in China, and Dogen Zenji give to each of the precepts.
*The first grave precept, not killing.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of everlasting dharma, not giving rise to concepts of killing is called the precept of not killing.
Dogen Zenji said, the Buddha seat grows in accordance with not taking life.
Transmit the life of Buddha's wisdom and do not kill.*
*The second grave precept, not stealing.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of unattainable dharma, not having thoughts of gaining is called the precept of not stealing.
Dogen Zenji said, the self and the things of the world are just as they are.
The gate of emancipation is open.*
*The third grave precept, not misusing sex.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of the ungilded dharma, not creating a veneer of attachment is called the precept of not misusing sex.
Dogen Zenji said, the three wheels are pure and clear.
When you have nothing to desire, you follow the way of all Buddhas.*
*The fourth grave precept, not lying.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of the inexplicable dharma, not preaching a single word is called the precept of not lying.
Dogen Zenji said, the dharma wheel turns from the beginning.
There is neither surplus nor lack.
The whole universe is moistened with nectar, and the truth is ready to harvest.*
*The fifth grave precept, not giving or taking drugs.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of the intrinsically pure dharma, not giving rise to delusions is called the precept of not giving or taking drugs.
Dogen Zenji said, drugs are not brought in yet.
Don't let them invade.
That is the great light.*
*The sixth grave precept, not discussing faults of others.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of one flawless dharma, not expounding upon error is called the precept of not speaking of faults of others.
Dogen Zenji said, in the Buddha dharma there is one path, one dharma, one realization, one practice.
Don't permit fault finding.
Don't permit haphazard talk.*
*The seventh precept, not praising yourself while abusing others.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of equitable dharma, not dwelling upon I against you is called the precept of not praising yourself while abusing others.
Dogen Zenji said, Buddhas and ancestral teachers realize the empty sky and the great earth.
When they manifest the noble body, there is neither inside nor outside in emptiness.
When they manifest the dharma body, there is not even a bit of earth on the ground.*
*The eighth grave precept, not sparing the dharma assets.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the genuine all-pervading dharma, not being stingy about a single thing is called the precept of not sparing the dharma assets.
Dogen Zenji said, one phrase, one verse, that is a ten thousand things and one hundred grasses.
One dharma, one realization.
That is all Buddhas and ancestral teachers.
Therefore, from the beginning, there has been no stinginess at all.*
*The ninth grave precept, not indulging in anger.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of selfless dharma, not contriving reality for the self is called the precept of not indulging in anger.
Dogen Zenji said, not advancing, not retreating, not real, not empty.
There is an ocean of bright clouds.
There is an ocean of solemn clouds.*
*The tenth grave precept, not defaming the three treasures.
Bodhidharma said, self-nature is subtle and mysterious.
In the realm of the one, not holding dualistic concepts of ordinary beings and sages is called the precept of not defaming the three treasures.
Dogen Zenji said, the teisho of the actual body is the harbor and the weir.
This is the most important thing in the world.
Its virtue finds its home in the ocean of essential nature.
It is beyond explanation.
We just accept it with respect and credit to it.*
**Participant:** Read that again, Chris.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** *Dogen Zenji said, the teisho of the actual body is the harbor and the weir.
This is the most important thing in the world.
Its virtue finds its home in the ocean of essential nature.
It is beyond explanation.
We just accept it with respect and credit to it.*
I hope you find something useful in these words.
If you don't, please do your best to forget everything I said.
Thank you so much for listening.
May I do everything in the truth this way.
